findings.heading: Testing your for loop
findings.proposition: The English carries '### Testing your for loop' as a rendered level-3 heading; the Spanish writes '###Probar tu bucle for  {.unnumbered}' with no space after the hashes, so it is not a heading at all.
findings.reader_consequence: The Spanish reader sees the literal string '###Probar tu bucle for {.unnumbered}' as body text, gets no table-of-contents entry for testing a for loop, and the testing advice appears to belong to the preceding 'Impresion' section.

findings.heading: Core components / Componentes basicos
findings.proposition: The English gives the for-loop syntax skeleton as R code, `for (item in sequence) {do operations using item}`, keeping the R keyword `in`; the Spanish replaces the skeleton with Spanish prose inside the same code span, `for (para cada elemento de la secuencia) {hacer operaciones con el elemento}`, which contains no `in` keyword.
findings.reader_consequence: A Spanish reader learning the syntax from this line never sees the required R keyword `in`, and the next sentence tells them to note the parentheses and curly brackets of a template that is not valid R.

findings.heading: Sequence / Secuencia
findings.proposition: The English states the basic structure of a sequence statement is `item in vector`, using the R keyword `in`; the Spanish states it is `elemento en el vector`, replacing the keyword `in` with the Spanish preposition `en`.
findings.reader_consequence: A Spanish reader takes `en` to be the R keyword and writes `for (i en x)`, which is a syntax error.

findings.heading: Sequence / Secuencia
findings.proposition: The English shows the first and second iteration values as `hospital_names[[1]]` and `hospital_names[[2]]` with matched double brackets; the Spanish shows `hospital_names[1]]` and `hospital_names[2]]`, with one opening bracket and two closing brackets.
findings.reader_consequence: A Spanish reader copies a malformed subsetting expression that errors, and the chapter's own rule that double brackets `[[ ]]` are used for indexing is contradicted where it is first demonstrated.

findings.heading: Sequence / Secuencia
findings.proposition: The English example is `for (i in seq_along(hospital_names) {OPERATIONS CODE}`; the Spanish example is `for (i en seq_along(nombres_de_hospital) {Codigo_de_operaciones}`, replacing the R keyword `in` with `en` and naming an object `nombres_de_hospital` that is never created anywhere in the chapter.
findings.reader_consequence: A Spanish reader who runs this line gets a syntax error from `en` and then an object-not-found error, because the code chunks in the same section define `hospital_names`, not `nombres_de_hospital`.

findings.heading: Looping plots / Bucles con graficos
findings.proposition: The English says the loop produces a separate plot for each hospital's cases, that is one plot per hospital; the Spanish says 'un grafico separado para cada caso del hospital', that is one plot per case of the hospital.
findings.reader_consequence: A Spanish reader expects one epicurve per case and cannot reconcile that with the loop below, which iterates over `hospital_names` and prints one plot per hospital.

findings.heading: map()
findings.proposition: The English tilde example is `map(.x = my_list, .f = ~mean(., na.rm = T))`; the Spanish writes `map(.x = mi_lista, .f = \~mean(., na.rm = T))`, with a backslash before the tilde inside the code span.
findings.reader_consequence: The rendered Spanish code shows a backslash before the tilde, so a reader copying the only tilde-syntax example in this bullet pastes a character R rejects, in the same sentence that tells them to use the tilde `~`.

findings.heading: Example - import and combine Excel sheets / Ejemplo: importar y combinar hojas de Excel
findings.proposition: The English names the first sheet "Central Hospital", the value actually held in `sheet_names`; the Spanish names it "Hospital Central", while leaving "Military Hospital" untranslated in the same sentence.
findings.reader_consequence: The Spanish reader compares the sentence with the printed `sheet_names` output two chunks above, which lists "Central Hospital", and cannot tell which spelling to pass to `which = ` or to `linelist_split[[...]]`.

findings.heading: Export as CSV files / Exportar como archivos CSV
findings.proposition: The English bullet writes the indexing expression as `linelist_split[[.x]]`; the Spanish writes it as a broken span, `linelist`_split[.x]], splitting the object name and losing one opening bracket.
findings.reader_consequence: The Spanish reader sees a mangled expression at the exact point the text explains how `.x` indexes the list, so the mechanism the bullet exists to teach is not legible.

findings.heading: Mapping a function across columns / Mapear una funcion a traves de las columnas
findings.proposition: The English says the element made of two or more sub-elements (`mean in group f` and `mean in group m`) is `estimate`; the Spanish attributes those two sub-elements to `conf.int` instead.
findings.reader_consequence: A Spanish reader looks for the group means under `conf.int`, and is then contradicted by the later section which correctly extracts them with `map(., "estimate")`.

findings.heading: Convert list to data frame / Convertir una lista en un dataframe
findings.proposition: The English names the two sub-elements of `estimate` as `mean in group f` and `mean in group m`, the literal names R returns; the Spanish renames them `media en el grupo f` and `media en el grupo m`.
findings.reader_consequence: A Spanish reader searching the printed `unnest_wider(means)` output, whose column names are the English strings, does not find the names the text told them to expect.

findings.heading: Convert list to data frame / Convertir una lista en un dataframe
findings.proposition: The English says `hoist()` acts like `unnest_wider()` but you specify which elements to unnest; the Spanish says you specify which elements are to be annulled ('se van a anular').
findings.reader_consequence: A Spanish reader understands `hoist()` as a way to delete list elements rather than to un-nest selected ones, and will not reach for it when they need to lift specific elements out of a list-column.
